en: Title: *Mārajitstotra Author: Harṣa Source: Hahn 1996 (essentially two verses from the *Nāgānanda*)
Tibetan:
D 1117 || The Praise to the Subduer of Māra is contained herein. Homage to the Three Jewels!

Having resorted to the pretext of meditation, what woman do you contemplate? Open your eyes for a moment and look at these people afflicted by the arrows of the bodiless god; though you are their protector, you do not protect them.
You are a hypocrite in your compassion—what man could be more merciless than you?

May the Victor, who was told by the wives of Māra, "He is full of envy," protect you— He who, having been asked what he intended regarding his meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), looked on with well-opened eyes for a moment.
If even the Protector does not guard us beings who are tormented by the bodiless arrow, [what else can be done?]
O Compassionate One, there is no other person more wretched than you, who have fallen into such perversion.
Although that jealous wife of Māra spoke thus, the Victorious Protector attained awakening.
Moreover: Furthermore,
having drawn his bow with desire, by the heroic Māras who leaped about like beaten, sharp-sounding drums—

May the Lord of Sages protect you—he who was seen remaining unshakable upon attaining enlightenment, while being gazed upon by celestial women with eyes turned toward him in smiles, yawns, and trembling frowns; by the Siddhas with their heads bowed low; and by Vāsava, his body bristling with joy out of wonder.
By the power of desire, another swift Māra, Pataha, who possesses a resonant voice, has drawn his bow everywhere.
By means of those who are like a hero with moving eyebrows, or like one who blinks, and who are devoid of grace, smiles, and playfulness;
Having seen that he was unable to move the Lord of Sages, the Protector, from his meditative concentration before he had attained enlightenment, [the Māras despaired].
With their hair standing on end from wonder, the perfected ones bow down with their most excellent limbs.
Though their matted locks were disheveled and their tongues protruded, as they were tormented, their minds did not become deranged.
The Māras of the gods of Radiance hold in their hands the finest peaks, as well as elephants, horses, and lions with faces.
Those whose deer-like faces have become as numerous as blades of grass, yet who have not become terrified by saṃsāra—
He is the Protector who is unmixed with the aspect of harming anyone—the Buddha, the Lord of Sages, the Eye of the World.
The Praise to the Subduer of Māra, composed by the venerable Rab dga’i lha, is complete.
